lessons.title: Clear vowels inside consonant–vowel patterns
lessons.objective: Change vowel shape inside ma mé mi mo mou, then transfer the same movements into other consonant rows and real words.
lessons.explanation:
Keep each vowel clear inside ma, mé, mi, mo, mou. Notice the tongue moving forward for mi and back with rounded lips for mou, and keep mé tense with no English glide.
The m row
ma · mé · mi · mo · mou
Close both lips for m, then open into the vowel. These are practice syllables, not five vocabulary words.
lips
Both lips meet
The tongue prepares for the next vowel; the lips make the closure.
Air passes through the nose during m.
Voice on
Say mmm → ma, then mé, mi, mo, mou. Open from the same light lip closure each time.
Keep the nasal m audible before the vowel, and keep mé and mo pure: no English glide into may or moh.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, change vowel shape inside ma mé mi mo mou, then transfer the same movements into other consonant rows and real words. Use the scene: A map at home. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: Keep the o round and steady to the end; do not let it slide into an English "oh-w".
The final t is silent: [mo].
ou is a single rounded vowel [mou], with no w sound after it. The final -sse is a clear s.

lessons.title: The m row: u and ou
lessons.objective: Say mu and mou clearly, with rounded lips for both, without changing the m.
lessons.explanation:
Let the lips close lightly for m while the following vowel changes. Compare mu and mou: both are rounded, but u keeps the tongue forward and ou pulls it back.
The m row
ma · mu · mi · mo · mou
Close both lips for m, then open into the vowel. Both mu and mou need rounded lips; only the tongue changes.
lips
Both lips meet
For mu the tongue stays forward as for mi; for mou it pulls back as for mo.
Air passes through the nose during m.
Voice on
Say mmm → mi, then mi → mu (keep the tongue, round the lips), then mu → mou (pull the tongue back).
Do not turn mu into mou: le mur and la moule must sound different.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, say mu and mou clearly, with rounded lips for both, without changing the m. Use the scene: A morning with Maxime. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: u: say "ee" with tightly rounded lips. Compare l'amour, where ou keeps the tongue back.
The ending -aie is an open è: [la-mo-nè]. The nn is a single n sound.
ou keeps the tongue back: [la-moul]. Compare le mur, where u is far forward.

lessons.title: The p row
lessons.objective: Practise a brief p release with less aspiration than a stressed English p.
lessons.explanation:
Make a small lip closure and release into pa, pé, pi, po, pou. French p carries almost no puff of air; keep the vowels distinct and add nothing after the release.
The p row
pa · pé · pi · po · pou
Close both lips, release, then say the vowel. Avoid a strong English-style puff of air.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
The tongue prepares for the vowel. Keep the lip closure brief.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say pa three times slowly, then pa → pi → pou. Feel the release with a hand in front of the mouth.
French p has almost no puff at all; do not force one, and do not add a vowel after it.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, practise a brief p release with less aspiration than a stressed English p. Use the scene: Buying fruit. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: ain is one nasal vowel: [pin]. No n is pronounced.

lessons.title: The t row
lessons.objective: Find the French dental t placement.
lessons.explanation:
Lightly touch the back of the upper front teeth for t. Practise ta, té, ti, to, tou and return to normal rhythm in Thérèse boit du thé.
The t row
ta · té · ti · to · tou
Place the tongue tip against the back of the upper front teeth. Release into the vowel without a strong puff of air.
teeth
Tongue tip at the upper front teeth
Use a light contact on the teeth themselves, not on the ridge behind them; release into the vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ta → ti → tou slowly. Notice the dental contact rather than an English-style ridge contact.
Avoid a strong puff or an extra vowel after t. The th in thé is just a t.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, find the French dental t placement. Use the scene: Tea with Thérèse. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: th is a plain t; é is short and tense, with no "y" glide at the end.
Both the p and the s are silent: [tan]. The vowel is nasal.
Thé + ière: [té-yèr]. Keep the t light and dental; the final r is spoken but very soft.

lessons.title: The n and l rows
lessons.objective: Keep the consonant distinct while changing vowels.
lessons.explanation:
Alternate na, né, ni, no, nou and la, lé, li, lo, lou. Keep nasal airflow for n and side airflow for l, and keep the l clear and light in every position.
The n row
na · né · ni · no · nou
Let air pass through the nose for n, then move into the vowel.
teeth
Tongue tip at the back of the upper front teeth
Make a light closure; prepare the next vowel without pressing hard.
Air passes through the nose during n.
Voice on
Say nnn → na, then na → ni → nou. Release the tongue into each vowel.
Do not let n turn into a nasal vowel before another vowel: la nuit has a clear n.
The l row
la · lé · li · lo · lou
Touch the ridge behind the upper teeth with the tongue tip and let air pass around the sides.
ridge
Tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper front teeth; sides leave space for airflow
Keep the tongue tip forward and the body of the tongue high and flat; the l stays light.
Oral airflow around the sides of the tongue.
Voice on
Say la → li → lou, then la lune → le lit → la lampe. Notice the vowel change without losing the l.
Never darken the l as in English ball: French l is clear in every position, including at the end of a word.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, keep the consonant distinct while changing vowels. Use the scene: A note beside the lamp. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: Keep the tongue tip forward on the n; the final e is silent.
am before p is a nasal vowel with no separate m sound, followed by a clear p. The final e is silent.
The final t is silent, and the l stays clear and light: [li].

lessons.title: The s and f rows
lessons.objective: Carry a continuous consonant into a steady vowel.
lessons.explanation:
Keep continuous airflow through sa, sé, si, so, sou and fa, fé, fi, fo, fou. Use the tongue groove for s and light lip-to-teeth narrowing for f; ph is simply f.
The s row
sa · sé · si · so · sou
Make a continuous s, then move into the vowel. A single s between vowels turns into z (lesson 14).
ridge
Tongue approaches the ridge; a narrow channel remains
Do not seal the mouth; form a groove and leave space for airflow.
Continuous oral airflow.
Voice off
Say sss → sa, then sa → si → sou. Keep the beginning continuous.
This is a narrowing target, not a complete contact. ss and a leading s both give the same clear s.
The f row
fa · fé · fi · fo · fou
Rest the lower lip lightly at the upper front teeth and let air flow through the narrow gap.
lip-teeth
Upper front teeth near the lower lip
Leave a small opening instead of biting the lip.
Continuous oral airflow through the gap.
Voice off
Say fff → fa, then fa → fi → fou with a gentle, continuous beginning.
Keep the lip contact light and the airflow steady. ph in la photo is the same f.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, carry a continuous consonant into a steady vowel. Use the scene: Soup and a photograph. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: The on is a nasal vowel with no spoken n: [sa-lon]. Keep the first s continuous.
ph is a plain f: [fo-to]. Keep the o round and steady.
-ille sounds like i plus a y glide: [fa-miy]. There is no l sound, and the final e is silent.
The r is made at the back of the mouth; the è is open, and the final r is soft.

lessons.title: One /k/ sound, several spellings
lessons.objective: Coordinate the back-of-tongue closure and vowel transition in /k/ patterns, then transfer into clear words and phrases.
lessons.explanation:
Use the back of the tongue for k in ca, qué, qui, co, cou. Read the French spellings c, qu and k; keep sound cues separate from spelling.
The /k/ sound row
ca · qué · qui · co · cou
One sound, several spellings: c before a/o/u, qu before e/i, k in a few words. The u in qué and qui is silent.
velar
Back of tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the tongue back closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ka → ki → kou → ké → ko slowly. Start each vowel with a small tongue-back closure and release; avoid a large English-style puff.
Do not use the tongue tip for k. The closure location adjusts naturally with the vowel.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, coordinate the back-of-tongue closure and vowel transition in /k/ patterns, then transfer into clear words and phrases. Use the scene: A small café order. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: qu is a plain k, with no w sound: [kinz]. The in is a nasal vowel.
The p is silent in comptoir: [kon-twar]. The om is a nasal vowel.
The final -que is a k with no vowel after it: [ki-osk].

lessons.title: One /g/ sound, two spellings
lessons.objective: Read hard g before all five vowels.
lessons.explanation:
Practise ga, gué, gui, go, gou after a pause. One sound, two spellings: g before a, o, u and gu before e and i. Never replace the silent u in gue and gui with an extra vowel.
The /g/ sound row
ga · gué · gui · go · gou
For this row, g before a/o/u and gu before e/i. The u in gué and gui is silent.
velar
Back of tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the tongue back closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice on
Say ga after a pause, then la gare and le guide. Keep the same firm g each time.
ge and gi belong with the j sound (lesson 19). With gu the u is silent: le guide is not [gou-ide].

oû is the same [ou] sound as in goutte. The t is silent.

lessons.title: Ch, gn, and vowel review
lessons.objective: Build ch and gn from a model without turning them into letter names.
lessons.explanation:
Make the smooth friction of ch (never "tch"), then the palatal nasal in gn. Use cha, ché, chi, cho, chou and gna, gné, gni, gno, gnou before real words.
The ch row
cha · ché · chi · cho · chou
Slide the air through a narrow channel for ch, with no closure and no t in front. Practise the syllables, then use meaningful words.
postalveolar
Tongue blade just behind the ridge, lips slightly rounded
Raise the tongue blade toward the roof of the mouth and leave a narrow passage.
Continuous friction, like a soft hush.
Voice off
Say chhh → cha, then cha → chi → chou. Keep the friction smooth from start to finish.
Do not say tch as in English church: French ch is only the friction.
The gn row
gna · gné · gni · gno · gnou
Raise the tongue body toward the hard palate and let air flow through the nose; then release into the vowel.
palate
Tongue body toward the hard palate
Use one palatal nasal gesture rather than a separate n plus a y, as in la montagne.
Air passes through the nose.
Voice on
Say gna slowly, then gna → gni → gnou; move into montagne and campagne with a model.
The tongue-body target matters more than an English spelling approximation such as ny.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, build ch and gn from a model without turning them into letter names. Use the scene: A child and a small backpack. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: ch is a soft hush, not "tch". ien is [yin]: the i is a short glide into a nasal vowel.
au is one o sound and the final d is silent: [cho]. Keep ch smooth, with no t in front.
gn sounds like the ny in canyon, one sound: [mon-ta-ny]. The final e is silent.

lessons.title: One nasal sound, two spellings: an and en
lessons.objective: Recognize that an and en are spelled differently but make one nasal vowel, with no n sound.
lessons.explanation:
Compare an in blanc and grand with en in lent and la menthe: different spellings, one nasal vowel. Before a consonant the n is not pronounced; before b or p it is written m (la chambre, le temps), with the same vowel.

lessons.title: H muet and h aspiré
lessons.objective: Read common silent h words without inserting a consonant, and spot h aspiré.
lessons.explanation:
The French h is never pronounced, but it comes in two kinds. With h muet, as in l'hôtel and l'heure, the word acts as if it starts with a vowel, so elision and liaison happen. With h aspiré, as in le hall and le héros, it acts as if it starts with a consonant: no l' and no liaison.
Silent h: the vowel stands alone
ha · hé · hi · ho · hou
Ignore the h completely and start straight on the vowel: ha is a, hé is é, hi is i, ho is o and hou is ou.
vowel
Open mouth; the tongue goes straight to the vowel position
Begin the vowel at once, with no breath or catch of air before it.
Oral airflow goes straight into the vowel.
Voice on
Say ha → a, hé → é, then l'hôtel → l'heure → l'habitude.
Do not add an English h-breath. Check the h aspiré words le hall and le héros: no l' and no liaison, so say les halls with no z.

sta · sté · sti · sto · stou
Start the s and move straight into the t with no vowel between them, then release into the vowel.

lessons.title: Nasal vowel or spoken n
lessons.objective: Notice when n makes a nasal vowel and when it is spoken before a vowel.
lessons.explanation:
Compare an and Anne, bon and bonne, voisin and voisine. Before a consonant or at the end of a word, the n disappears into a nasal vowel; before a vowel it is a normal spoken n. Practise on, in, an and un as nasals.
The nasal vowels
pan · bon · pin · brun · loin
Say the vowel with air flowing through the nose and the mouth together; the tongue never closes on an n.
nasal vowel
Soft palate lowered, so air goes through the nose and mouth
Keep the tongue in the vowel position and do not close on an n or ng.
Air flows through the nose and the mouth at once.
Voice on
Say pan → bon → pin → brun, then compare an → Anne, bon → bonne, voisin → voisine.
Do not finish with an n or ng sound. When a vowel or a doubled n follows, the vowel turns oral and the n is spoken: Anne, bonne, voisine.

lessons.objective: Keep pr, br and fr together with the French r and add no vowel in between.
lessons.explanation:
Move through pr, br and fr in real words (prix, bras, frère) without inserting a vowel inside the consonant cluster. Join the French r straight to the first consonant and release into one clear following vowel.
The p row
pa · pé · pi · po · pou
Close both lips, release, then say the vowel. Avoid a strong English-style puff of air.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
The tongue prepares for the vowel. Keep the lip closure brief.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say pa three times slowly, then pa → pi → pou. Feel the release with a hand in front of the mouth.
Use less aspiration than an English p; do not force a puff. In clusters such as pr and pl, join the next consonant straight to the p.
The b row
ba · bé · bi · bo · bou
Close both lips and voice the sound from the start, then open into the vowel. B is always a full two-lip closure; v is a separate lip-teeth sound.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
Keep the lips light and the closure brief. Do not turn b into the lip-teeth v.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice on
Say ba after a pause, then bé → bi → bou, then bras and librairie with the r joined to the b.
Do not confuse b with v: bal and val are different words. The b stays the same in every position.

ara · éré · iri · oro · ourou
Make the same back-of-the-tongue friction between two vowels, with no tongue-tip tap; keep the friction light and brief.
uvula

Keep the tip down and let the back of the tongue narrow the channel for a moment, then return to the vowel.
Brief, light friction in the oral airflow.

Say ara → éré → iri, then prix, bras and frère with the r joined to the consonant before it.
Do not tap or roll the r; it is made at the back of the mouth. Add no extra vowel before or after it.

teeth

teeth

ara · éré · iri · oro · ourou

uvula

lessons.title: Cr and gr clusters
lessons.objective: Build a k-to-r and g-to-r cluster in real words.
lessons.explanation:
Practise cr and gr in real words: crème, croix, grand, groupe, gris. Keep the cluster compact, with the French r right after the k or g sound, then say a complete phrase with ordinary rhythm.
The /k/ sound row
ca · qué · qui · co · cou
One sound, several spellings: c before a, o, u; qu before e, i; k. The u in qué and qui is silent.
velar
Back of the tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the back of the tongue closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ka → ki → kou → ké → ko slowly, then crème and croix with the r joined to the k.
Do not use the tongue tip for k, and avoid a large English-style puff of air.
The /g/ sound row
ga · gué · gui · go · gou
Start with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, voice the sound and release. Write g before a, o, u and gu before e, i; the u in gué and gui is silent.
velar
Back of the tongue at the soft palate
Keep the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth while the back of the tongue closes and releases.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice on
Say ga → gué → gui → go → gou, then grand and groupe with the r joined to the g.
Use ga gué gui go gou for the hard g. Ge and gi belong with j, a different sound.
The French r between vowels
ara · éré · iri · oro · ourou
Make the same back-of-the-tongue friction between two vowels, with no tongue-tip tap; keep the friction light and brief.
uvula
Back of the tongue near the uvula
Keep the tip down and let the back of the tongue narrow the channel for a moment, then return to the vowel.
Brief, light friction in the oral airflow.
Voice on
Say ara → éré → iri, then crème, grand and gris with the r joined to the consonant before it.
Do not tap or roll the r; it is made at the back of the mouth. Add no extra vowel before or after it.

lessons.title: Clusters with l, including final -ble/-ple/-cle
lessons.objective: Keep pl, bl, fl, cl and gl as clusters, and the final -ble, -ple and -cle without a vowel.
lessons.explanation:
Practise pla, plé, pli, plo, plou, then switch to bl, fl, cl and gl with the same vowel order. Keep the l joined to the consonant before it, and in final -ble, -ple and -cle (la table, simple, l'oncle) say the l with no vowel after it.
The p row
pa · pé · pi · po · pou
Close both lips, release, then say the vowel. Avoid a strong English-style puff of air.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
The tongue prepares for the vowel. Keep the lip closure brief.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say pa three times slowly, then pa → pi → pou, then plat and place with the l joined to the p.
Use less aspiration than an English p; do not force a puff. In clusters such as pr and pl, join the next consonant straight to the p.
The b row
ba · bé · bi · bo · bou
Close both lips and voice the sound from the start, then open into the vowel. B is always a full two-lip closure; v is a separate lip-teeth sound.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
Keep the lips light and the closure brief. Do not turn b into the lip-teeth v.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice on
Say ba after a pause, then bé → bi → bou, then blanc and table with the l joined to the b.
Do not confuse b with v: bal and val are different words. The b stays the same in every position.
The f row
fa · fé · fi · fo · fou
Rest the upper front teeth lightly on the lower lip and let air flow through the narrow gap. F is also spelled ph, as in photo.
lip-teeth
Upper front teeth near the lower lip
Leave a small opening instead of biting the lip.
Continuous oral airflow through the gap.
Voice off
Say fff → fa, then fa → fi → fou, then fleur and frère.
Keep the lip contact light and the airflow steady. Do not turn f into p.
The /k/ sound row
ca · qué · qui · co · cou
One sound, several spellings: c before a, o, u; qu before e, i; k. The u in qué and qui is silent.
velar
Back of the tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the back of the tongue closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ka → ki → kou → ké → ko slowly, then classe with the l joined to the k.
Do not use the tongue tip for k, and avoid a large English-style puff of air.
The /g/ sound row
ga · gué · gui · go · gou
Start with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, voice the sound and release. Write g before a, o, u and gu before e, i; the u in gué and gui is silent.
velar
Back of the tongue at the soft palate
Keep the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth while the back of the tongue closes and releases.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice on
Say ga → gué → gui → go → gou, then glace with the l joined to the g.
Use ga gué gui go gou for the hard g. Ge and gi belong with j, a different sound.
The l row
la · lé · li · lo · lou
Touch the ridge behind the upper teeth with the tongue tip and let air pass around the sides.
ridge
Tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper front teeth
Keep the l light and clear, with the tongue tip forward; it is the same l in every position.
Oral airflow around the sides of the tongue.
Voice on
Say la → li → lou, then plat → blanc → fleur → classe → glace.
Do not use the dark English l, even at the end of a word, and do not add an extra vowel before the l.

lessons.explanation:

The t row
ta · té · ti · to · tou
Place the tongue tip against the back of the upper front teeth. Release into the vowel without a strong puff of air; th is simply t in French.
teeth
Tongue tip/blade at the upper front teeth
Use a light contact near the back of the upper teeth; release into the vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ta → ti → tou slowly. Notice the dental contact rather than an English-style ridge contact.
Avoid a strong puff or an extra vowel after t.

lessons.title: Regional listening: southern France
lessons.objective: Recognize examples from named regions without mixing every feature.
lessons.explanation:
Keep a consistent production model for standard French and compare named regional examples (southern France: spoken final e, nasal vowels ending in a light ng) only when real reviewed audio is available. Without those clips, use this as a transcript and discussion task, not a listening test.
The y glide
ya · yé · yo · ille · aille
Raise the front of the tongue toward the hard palate for a short glide into the vowel. The glide is spelled y, ill or il: yeux, fille, travail.
palate
Tongue body approaches the hard palate
Keep the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth and glide quickly into the next vowel.
Oral airflow with a light constriction.
Voice on
Say ya → yo, then fille → travail → soleil, each with the same quick glide.
Ville, mille and tranquille keep a plain l. Regional realizations are valid; do not mark them as wrong.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, recognize examples from named regions without mixing every feature. Use the scene: Different voices, the same street. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: The x is silent: [vwa].
g before i is the soft zh: [ré-jyon].
The è is open; the l is spoken and the final e is silent: [mo-dèl].
-ille is [iy] here: [fa-miy].

lessons.title: Regional listening: Quebec, Belgium and Switzerland
lessons.objective: Recognize selected variations in real, reviewed recordings.
lessons.explanation:
Compare regional forms only with identified speaker examples: Quebec tu and dire with a light ts or dz, septante and nonante in Belgium and Switzerland. Keep your own standard production model; regional forms are for listening, and none of them is wrong.
J and soft g
ja · gé · gi · jo · jou
Make a continuous buzzing zh, like the s in measure. It is spelled j, or g before e/i.
postalveolar
Tongue blade just behind the ridge, lips slightly rounded
Raise the blade behind the ridge and leave a narrow channel for the air.
Continuous oral airflow with friction.
Voice on
Say jjj → ja, then ja → gé → gi → jo → jou, then le jardin.
Do not start with a d: jardin is not djardin.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, recognize selected variations in real, reviewed recordings. Use the scene: Recognizing a familiar message. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: The x is silent: [vwa].
The j is a soft zh, never dj, and -in is a nasal vowel.
Liaison: the s of les links to the vowel as z: [lé-za-mi].
x is ks: [kon-tèkst]; the final -e is silent but the t is spoken.

lessons.title: Personal sound priorities
lessons.objective: Choose two recurring pronunciation habits from real evidence.
lessons.explanation:
Select two priorities from real self-listening or instructor observations. Use the relevant consonant-and-vowel row, then test the movement in a new phrase instead of drilling everything faster.
The m row
ma · mé · mi · mo · mou
Close both lips for m, then open into the vowel. These are practice syllables, not five vocabulary words.
lips
Both lips meet
The tongue prepares for the next vowel; the lips make the closure.
Air passes through the nose during m.
Voice on
Say mmm → ma, then mé, mi, mo, mou. Open from the same light lip closure each time.
Keep the nasal m audible before the vowel.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, choose two recurring pronunciation habits from real evidence. Use the scene: Two priorities for the next practice. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: The h is silent: [la-bi-tud]. The u is the tightly rounded ee.
ph is f: [fraz].
ai at the end is [è]: [lé-sè].
Nasal, then è, then nasal: [lan-trèn-man]. The circumflex on aî does not change the sound, and the e after n drops.

lessons.title: Conversation under a complication
lessons.objective: Maintain clear speech when a scene changes unexpectedly.
lessons.explanation:
Warm up with ca qui cou qué co, then handle a complication without a script. Preserve the important consonants, numbers, and phrase boundaries while deciding what to do.
The /k/ sound row
ca · qué · qui · co · cou
One sound, different spellings: c before a/o/u; qu before e/i. The u in qué and qui is silent.
velar
Back of tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the tongue back closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ca → qué → qui → co → cou slowly. Start each vowel with a small tongue-back closure and release; avoid a large English-style puff.
Do not use the tongue tip for k. The closure location adjusts naturally with the vowel.
lessons.speakingPrompt: In French, maintain clear speech when a scene changes unexpectedly. Use the scene: An unexpected change during a call. Ask a follow-up question and close by confirming the meaning. Keep one sound target clear; a correct transcript is not proof of pronunciation.

items.note: The d is a full closure and the final -e is silent: [la-drès].
ch is sh, an and -ent are nasal vowels, and the final t is silent: [chanj-man].
pp is a single p and the final l is spoken: [la-pèl].
ch is sh and the x is silent: [chwa].

lessons.title: Final transfer portfolio
lessons.objective: Compare baseline and final speech using a clear review rubric.
lessons.explanation:
Choose your own consonant-and-vowel warm-up, then compare baseline and final speech with specific observations. Use a new reading and an unexpected question; completion alone is not an assessed native accent.
The French r at the start of a word
ra · ré · ri · ro · rou
Start the r at the back of the mouth: the back of the tongue rises toward the uvula and makes light friction. It is never rolled with the tongue tip.
uvula
Back of the tongue near the uvula
Keep the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth and let the back of the tongue make the narrow channel.
Continuous oral airflow with light friction.
Voice on
Say a gentle rrr → ra, then ra → ré → rou. Pause between attempts and use the model before adding speed.
The r is not a tight press or a trill; mark it as developing if it still sounds like an English r.
